extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IP litigators, and legal scholars interested in PTAB/AIA proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate eligibility, procedural rules, strategic advantages/risks, and recent case law affecting the Transitional Program for Covered Business Method (CBM) reviews under the America Invents Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered Business Method patent definition (Section 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: "a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service," but not a so-called "technological" invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory definition is the baseline for CBM eligibility. The Board initially interpreted "financial" broadly (relating generally to monetary matters), allowing patents outside traditional financial-industry contexts to qualify (e.g., Versata). Later Federal Circuit decisions narrowed that reading (see Unwired Planet, Secure Axcess) and criticized the "incidental or complementary" reach, emphasizing the statutory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner standing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Only parties actually sued or charged with infringement of the patent can initiate a Covered Business Method Review proceeding (Section 18(a)(1)(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This heightened standing was cited as a reason for modest early filing levels. Unlike some post-grant proceedings, CBM requires an actual charge of infringement before a petitioner may file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible grounds to challenge in CBM
rubrics_metrics.description: A CBM challenge can be based not only on patent and printed-publication prior art but also on failure to meet other grounds for patentability, including 35 U.S.C. § 101 (subject-matter eligibility), § 112 (indefiniteness), and double-patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a key advantage of CBM over IPR (which is limited to §102/§103 grounds based on patents/printed publications). Petitioners used CBM to bring §101 challenges (revived post-Alice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of estoppel after CBM
rubrics_metrics.description: CBM estoppel extends only to grounds actually asserted in the proceeding, and not to grounds that "reasonably could have been asserted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrower estoppel was touted as an advantage over IPR estoppel; however, caselaw and practice made the practical difference small because IPR estoppel (as applied) also left re-litigation opportunities for non-instituted grounds and claims. See comparisons with 35 U.S.C. §§ 315(e)(2), 325(e)(1)-(2) and relevant Federal Circuit cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 18(b)(1) stay-of-litigation factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18(b)(1) included a special factor for district courts to consider when evaluating a motion to stay in view of a pending CBM review, intended to favor stays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Congress and sponsors (e.g., Sen. Schumer) expected this to make stays near-automatic, in practice stays were granted only about 54% of the time early on. Federal Circuit and district-court timing considerations (e.g., VirtualAgility) limited the stay benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation variability across PTAB panels
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB panels varied in applying the CBM eligibility test—some panels adopted the broad Versata-style reading of "financial," while others declined to institute in similar cases, requiring more direct connection to financial products/services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel-to-panel inconsistency made institution predictions unreliable (described as a "coin toss"), discouraging petitioners. Examples: ServiceNow (denial) vs. Versata (grant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that at least one claim expressly recite a financial activity (Federal Circuit standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit held that the patent must have at least one claim that expressly recites a financial activity element; mere "incidental to" or "complementary to" financial activity is insufficient to make a patent a CBM patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key decisions: Unwired Planet (vacated Board's broader test), Secure Axcess and related rulings narrowing CBM reach. This limits CBM applicability and reduced new filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pre-institution disclaimers by patent owners
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners can cancel (disclaim) claims that support a challenger's assertion that the patent claims a "Covered Business Method," and a disclaimed claim is treated as if it never existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strategy allowed owners to end proceedings unilaterally pre-institution (37 C.F.R. § 42.207(e)). Post-institution disclaimers do not have the same effect because eligibility is determined at institution time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing rule for eligibility determination
rubrics_metrics.description: CBM eligibility is determined based on the claims of the challenged patent as they exist at the time of the institution decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, post-institution disclaimers do not affect the Board's CBM eligibility determination; petitioners and owners must consider claim status at institution moment (see J.P. Morgan Chase v. Intellectual Ventures II and Emerson Elec. examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial-institution / non-instituted-grounds estoppel consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, Final Written Decisions addressed only instituted grounds and claims; non-instituted grounds often were not subject to estoppel, allowing re-litigation of those grounds in district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice reduced the practical difference between CBM and IPR estoppel. The Supreme Court's SAS decision (requiring institution on all claims/all grounds) altered the landscape and may expand estoppel scope going forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness metrics for the CBM program (filings, institutions, success rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Program statistics used to assess CBM's effectiveness: e.g., sharp decline in petitions (36 petitions in FY2018), months with zero filings, increases in denials of institution after Federal Circuit narrowing; high invalidation rates reported for cases reaching Final Written Decision (statistics cited: ~96.7% or ~97% with some claims found unpatentable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics feed competing narratives: CBM succeeded in weeding out bad patents vs. CBM collapsed due to narrowings, costs, and practical limitations. Use multiple metrics (filings, institution rates, stay rates, invalidation rates) when evaluating program health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/cost consideration for challengers
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuing a CBM can be expensive (official fees alone cited at a minimum of $38,000), affecting challenger calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost must be weighed against benefits (ability to raise §101/§112 etc., narrower estoppel, stay likelihood). Combined costs and reduced practical advantages contributed to declining filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical litigation strategy implications (raising grounds, dual-forum tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners encouraged raising many grounds in IPR petitions because non-instituted grounds could be later pursued in district court; petitioners faced tradeoffs between PTAB petitions and district-court strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because IPR estoppel historically left non-instituted grounds available for district-court litigation, petitioners often broadened petitions. This interaction affected the perceived advantages of CBM and shaped filing strategies (and was affected by SAS and evolving caselaw).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory sunset and legislative context
rubrics_metrics.description: The CBM program was established as a transitional program under the AIA and was set to sunset on Sept. 16, 2020 (35 U.S.C. § 18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative attempts to extend or expand the program occurred (e.g., Senator Schumer proposals) but failed; sunset timing influenced practitioner and policymaker views on whether to invest in CBM petitions.
